name: Poykai Āḻvār
summary: First of the three 'first Āḻvārs' (Mutal Āḻvārkaḷ); author of the Mutal Tiruvantāti, which lights a lamp of the whole world for the discus-bearer and teaches that the Lord takes whatever form and name his devotees love.

tradition.text: born at the close of the Dvāpara age (hagiographies)

realization_account.text: Born, not of a womb, in a lotus in the temple tank (poykai) at Tiruveḵkā in Kāñcī. On a night of rain he sheltered in the narrow vestibule of a hermitage at Tirukkōvalūr — room for one to lie; Pūtattāḻvār came and they sat; Pēyāḻvār came and they stood; then a fourth pressed in among them unseen. Poykai lit a lamp with the earth as its bowl and the sea as its ghee and sang the first antāti; in the light the Lord was seen.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Counted by tradition as a descent (aṃśa) of the Lord's conch Pāñcajanya (low confidence; lists vary).

name: Pūtattāḻvār
summary: Second of the 'first Āḻvārs'; author of the Iraṇṭām Tiruvantāti, which lights the lamp of love, longing and a melting mind for Nāraṇaṉ.

tradition.text: born at the close of the Dvāpara age (hagiographies)

realization_account.text: Born in a flower at Tirukkaṭalmallai; at the Tirukkōvalūr meeting he lit the lamp of love with longing as ghee and his melting mind as wick.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Aṃśa of the mace Kaumodakī in the tradition's list (low confidence).

name: Pēyāḻvār
summary: Third of the 'first Āḻvārs'; author of the Mūṉṟām Tiruvantāti, which opens with the vision seen in the other two's lamps: 'I have seen Śrī, I have seen the golden form ...'. Called 'the mad one' for his ecstatic devotion; by tradition he turned Tirumaḻicai to Viṣṇu.

tradition.text: born at the close of the Dvāpara age (hagiographies)

realization_account.text: Born in a red lily in a well at Mylapore; at Tirukkōvalūr, by the light the others had kindled, he saw the Lord with Śrī, the golden form, the discus and the conch, and sang the third antāti.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Aṃśa of the sword Nandaka in the tradition's list (low confidence).

name: Tirumaḻicai Āḻvār
summary: Author of the Nāṉmukaṉ Tiruvantāti and the Tiruccanta Viruttam; the Āḻvār who, in the tradition's account, first studied the Buddhist, Jain and Śaiva doctrines and then found refuge in Nārāyaṇa; his verses insist that Nārāyaṇa created Brahmā and Brahmā Śiva.

tradition.text: born in the Dvāpara age and said to have lived some 4,700 years (hagiographies)

realization_account.text: Born to the sage Bhārgava as a limbless form, abandoned, quickened by the Lord and raised by a woodcutter's family; he passed through the Śākya, Jain and Śaiva teachings before Pēyāḻvār turned him to Viṣṇu. When the Pallava king banished his disciple Kaṇikaṇṇaṉ from Kāñcī, the Āḻvār told the Lord of Tiruveḵkā to roll up his serpent-bed and come too; the Lord did, and returned when they returned — hence 'the Lord who did as he was told' (coṉṉa vaṇṇam ceyta perumāḷ). He cast his writings into the Kāvēri and only two floated back against the current. At Kuṭantai the reclining Lord began to rise when the Āḻvār asked him to speak.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Aṃśa of the discus Sudarśana in the tradition's list (low confidence).

name: Nammāḻvār
summary: Chief of the Āḻvārs and 'first head of the clan' (kulapati) of the Śrīvaiṣṇavas: author of the Tiruviruttam, Tiruvāciriyam, Periya Tiruvantāti and Tiruvāymoḻi, held to be the four Vedas in Tamil. His hymns teach the Lord's supremacy and accessibility, knowledge-and-love as the Lord's gift, surrender at Tiruvēṅkaṭam with Śrī as mediator, service to the Lord and his devotees, and love-longing in the voice of Parāṅkuśa-nāyakī; the last decads describe the ascent on the path of light and final union.

tradition.text: born in the first year of the Kali age (hagiographies; one account gives the 43rd day)

realization_account.text: Born to Kāri and Uṭaiya Naṅkai of a Vellāḷa family at Kurukūr, the child did not cry or feed and repelled the 'śaṭha' wind that makes newborns forget (hence Śaṭhakopa); his parents laid him in a hollow of the tamarind tree at the temple, where he sat silent in absorption for sixteen years. Madhurakavi, following a light from the north, found him and asked: 'If the small is born in the body of the dead, what will it eat and where will it lie?' — the child answered: 'That it will eat, and there it will lie.' He then sang his four works, which Madhurakavi wrote down. Centuries later he appeared to Nāthamuni in vision and gave him the whole Prabandham.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Registry id. U14 references him as the head of the Śrīvaiṣṇava lineage. The 'small/dead' riddle is commonly read as the soul (small) born in matter (dead): it lives on matter's experiences until it knows the Lord. Aṃśa of Viṣvaksena in the tradition's list (moderate). His image-crown Śaṭhāri (caṭāri) bears the Lord's feet (prc:satari).

name: Madhurakavi Āḻvār
summary: Disciple of Nammāḻvār and author of the eleven-verse Kaṇṇinuṇ Ciṟuttāmpu, addressed to his teacher rather than to Viṣṇu: 'I know no other god'. The model of devotion to the teacher as sufficient (ācārya-niṣṭhā); he recorded Nammāḻvār's hymns.

realization_account.text: A brāhmaṇa of Tirukkōḷūr who, while at Ayodhyā on pilgrimage, saw a light in the southern sky, followed it to Kurukūr and found the silent Nammāḻvār under the tamarind; tested him with a riddle, received his answer, and served him for the rest of his life.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Kulaśekhara Āḻvār
summary: Cēra king of Kerala who renounced his throne for the company of devotees at Śrīraṅgam; author of the Tamil Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi and (by tradition) the Sanskrit Mukundamālā. His hymns ask to be born even as a fish or a step at Tiruvēṅkaṭam and cling to the Lord 'as a child pushed away by its mother still cries for her'.

scholarly.text: c. 9th c. CE (identification with the Cēra Kulaśekhara of Mahodayapuram is debated)

realization_account.text: So absorbed was the king in hearing the Rāmāyaṇa that when the reciter told of Rāma fighting Khara's fourteen thousand demons alone, he ordered his army to march to Rāma's aid. His ministers, resenting the devotees who thronged his court, accused them of stealing a jewel; he put his hand into a pot containing a cobra, declaring that the devotees could not steal, and was unharmed. He gave up his kingdom to live among devotees at Śrīraṅgam.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Aṃśa of the Kaustubha gem in the tradition's list (moderate). The threshold of the Tirupati sanctum is called 'Kulaśekharaṉ paṭi' after Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi 4.9.

name: Periyāḻvār
summary: Brāhmaṇa priest-gardener of Śrīvilliputtūr, foster-father of Āṇṭāḷ; author of the Tiruppallāṇṭu, which opens the Prabandham and daily worship with a benediction for the Lord's own safety, and of the Periyāḻvār Tirumoḻi, the first Tamil song-cycle of Kṛṣṇa's childhood sung through Yaśodā's eyes.

scholarly.text: c. 9th c. CE (contemporary with the Pāṇḍya Śrīmāṟa Śrīvallabha, r. c. 815–862, on one view)

realization_account.text: Summoned when the Pāṇḍya king Vallabhadeva sought to know the supreme truth, he established from the scriptures that Nārāyaṇa is supreme; the purse of gold hung as the prize bent down to him. The Lord appeared on Garuḍa in the sky to see his devotee honoured; fearing the evil eye might fall on the Lord, the Āḻvār sang 'many years, many years' for his safety.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Aṃśa of Garuḍa in the tradition's list (moderate).

name: Āṇṭāḷ
summary: The woman among the Āḻvārs: author of the Tiruppāvai, the thirty verses of the Mārkaḻi vow sung across South India, and the Nācciyār Tirumoḻi of bridal longing for Kṛṣṇa. She wore the Lord's garland before offering it and vowed to marry only the Lord; the tradition says she was wedded to Raṅganātha at Śrīraṅgam.
alt_names: Cūṭikkoṭutta Nācciyār ('the lady who gave after wearing')

scholarly.text: c. 9th c. CE (astronomical readings of Tiruppāvai 13 give dates in the 8th–9th c.)

realization_account.text: Found as an infant under a tulasī plant in Periyāḻvār's garden; as a girl she wore the garlands meant for the Lord and looked at herself in a well to see if she was a fit bride. Her father, discovering this, did not offer that garland; the Lord told him in a dream that he wanted only garlands she had worn. Refusing any mortal bridegroom, she was taken in bridal procession to Śrīraṅgam at the Lord's command and entered the image of Raṅganātha.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Held to be Bhūdevī (the Earth) descended; hence some lists omit her from the Āḻvārs as not a human soul. Some modern scholars have suggested Periyāḻvār composed in her name; the tradition rejects this.

name: Toṇṭaraṭippoṭi Āḻvār
summary: Garland-maker of Śrīraṅgam whose name means 'dust of the feet of the Lord's servants'; author of the Tirumālai and the dawn-awakening Tiruppaḷḷiyeḻucci. After a fall into a courtesan's household he was restored by the Lord's grace and taught that the name is sweeter than Indra's kingdom and that devotees of any birth are to be honoured.

realization_account.text: A brāhmaṇa devoted to making garlands for Raṅganātha, he was infatuated with the courtesan Dēvadēvi and lost all his wealth. The Lord, in the guise of a servant, sent her a golden vessel of the temple in Vipranārāyaṇa's name; he was arrested for its theft until the Lord revealed the truth in a dream to the king. Humbled, he returned to service and named himself dust of the feet of the devotees.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Aṃśa of the garland Vanamālā in the tradition's list (low confidence).

name: Tiruppāṇ Āḻvār
summary: Bard of the pāṇar community, held untouchable, who sang to Raṅganātha from across the Kāvēri until the priest Lokasāraṅga was commanded to carry him on his shoulders into the sanctum; there he sang the ten verses of Amalaṉātipirāṉ, describing the Lord from feet to face, and entered the Lord.

realization_account.text: Raised in a family of pāṇar bards at Uṟaiyūr, he would not set foot on the holy island and sang from the far bank. When Lokasāraṅga Muni, going for water for the Lord, found him in his way and struck him, the Lord bled and commanded the priest to carry the Āḻvār in on his shoulders. Seeing the Lord from feet to face, he sang that his eyes would see nothing else, and merged into the image.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Aṃśa of the Śrīvatsa mark in the tradition's list (low confidence).

name: Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār
summary: Chieftain of Tiruvāli-Tirunakari in the Cōḻa country, from the Kaḷḷar community, who turned from robbery to become the most prolific Āḻvār: author of the Periya Tirumoḻi, Tirukkuṟuntāṇṭakam, Tiruneṭuntāṇṭakam, Tiruveḻukkūṟṟirukkai and the two Maṭals (held to be the six aṅgas of the Tamil Veda). He sang some eighty sacred sites, the saving name Nārāyaṇa, and love-longing as Parakāla-nāyakī.

scholarly.text: c. 8th c. CE (praises the Pallava Nandivarman II Pallavamalla)

realization_account.text: A commander under the Cōḻa, he loved Kumudavalli, who would marry him only if he took the Vaiṣṇava marks and fed a thousand and eight devotees daily. To keep the vow he turned to robbing travellers, and waylaid a bridal party that was the Lord and Lakṣmī in disguise. Unable to pull the ring from the bridegroom's toe, he demanded the spell that held it; the Lord whispered into his ear the eight-syllable mantra, and he burst into the hymn of the name. He spent his wealth on the walls of Śrīraṅgam — by one story melting down a golden image taken from a Buddhist shrine at Nāgapaṭṭinam — and is credited with beginning the festival of reciting the Tiruvāymoḻi at Śrīraṅgam.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Aṃśa of the bow Śārṅga in the tradition's list (moderate). The Nāgapaṭṭinam image story is the hagiographies' and is recorded here as such.

name: Kaṇikaṇṇaṉ
summary: Disciple of Tirumaḻicai Āḻvār whose banishment from Kāñcī occasioned the story of the Lord who rolled up his serpent-bed and followed them.

realization_account.text: He refused to sing the Pallava king's praises, saying his tongue was for the Lord alone, and was banished.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Lokasāraṅga Muni
summary: Priest of the Śrīraṅgam temple who, at the Lord's command, carried Tiruppāṇ Āḻvār on his shoulders into the sanctum.

realization_account.text: Having struck the bard who stood in his path, he saw blood on the Lord's image and was told to carry the devotee in himself.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Kumudavalli
summary: Wife of Tirumaṅkai Āḻvār in the hagiographies, who made his taking the Vaiṣṇava marks and daily feeding of devotees the condition of their marriage — the occasion of his turning to God.

name: Kampaṉ
summary: Tamil poet of the Irāmāvatāram (Kamba Rāmāyaṇam), the great devotional retelling of Rāma's story; by tradition he also sang the Caṭakōpar Antāti in praise of Nammāḻvār so that his Rāmāyaṇa would be accepted at Śrīraṅgam.
notes: Not an Āḻvār; placed under lin:alvar as the lineage of Tamil Vaiṣṇava devotional poetry. Tradition: at the Rāmāyaṇa's first recital at Śrīraṅgam the Narasiṃha image roared approval.

name: Nārada
summary: U25 contribution: the divine sage to whom the Nārada Bhakti Sūtra is attributed ('spoken by Nārada', NBS 84); in NBS 19 his own definition of devotion is that all acts are offered to the Lord and forgetting him is supreme anguish.
notes: U25 contribution only; other units record the Upaniṣadic, epic and Purāṇic Nārada. Identity of the sūtra's author with those figures is the tradition's attribution, not asserted.

name: Śāṇḍilya
summary: U25 contribution: the sage to whom the Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra is attributed; in the Nārada Bhakti Sūtra (NBS 18) his definition of devotion is love 'not opposed to delight in the self'; in the Śāṇḍilya Sūtra he holds that devotion bears on both the Lord and the self (as recalled).
notes: U25 contribution only; identity with the Upaniṣadic Śāṇḍilya (ChU 3.14) and with the Pāñcarātra Śāṇḍilya is the tradition's, not asserted here.

name: Svapneśvara
summary: Author of the standard commentary (bhāṣya) on the Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra.

name: Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha
summary: U25 contribution: a Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha is credited with the Bhakticandrikā on the Śāṇḍilya Bhakti Sūtra; several authors share the name and the identification is uncertain.

name: Vopadeva
summary: U25 contribution: compiler of the Muktāphala, an arrangement of Bhāgavata verses under the themes of devotion, commented on by Hemādri.

name: Hemādri
summary: U25 contribution: minister of the Yādava kings who wrote the Kaivalyadīpikā commentary on his associate Vopadeva's Muktāphala.

name: Viṣṇupurī
summary: Compiler of the Bhaktiratnāvalī, an anthology of Bhāgavata verses on devotion with his own commentary Kāntimālā.
notes: Region (Tirhut) and date recalled with low confidence.

name: Garga
summary: Sage cited in the Nārada Bhakti Sūtra (NBS 17) for the definition of devotion as attachment to hearing the Lord's stories; named among the bhakti teachers (NBS 83). In the Purāṇas the family priest of the Yādavas who named Kṛṣṇa.

name: Jayadeva
summary: Sanskrit poet of the Gīta Govinda, the song-poem of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa's love in separation and union, sung daily before Jagannātha at Purī and revered by the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavas and in the temple music of Odisha, Bengal, Kerala and the south.
places: Kenduli / Kindubilva (claimed by Bengal and by Odisha as Kenduli Sasan)

realization_account.text: Son of Bhojadeva and Rāmādevī (the poem's closing verse). A wandering ascetic, he was given Padmāvatī in marriage by her father at Jagannātha's command. When he hesitated to write that Kṛṣṇa asked to place Rādhā's foot on his head, he went to bathe; Kṛṣṇa, in Jayadeva's form, came and wrote the line 'dehi pada-pallavam udāram' himself.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Birthplace disputed between Bengal (Kenduli, Birbhum), Odisha (Kenduli Sasan near Purī) and Mithilā. Two hymns attributed to him are in the Sikh Ādi Granth (context only). Distinct from the later Jayadeva of the Candrāloka.

name: Padmāvatī (wife of Jayadeva)
summary: Temple dancer dedicated to Jagannātha and wife of Jayadeva in the hagiographies; the Gīta Govinda calls its poet 'emperor of the dancers at Padmāvatī's feet' (GG 1.2), read by tradition as referring to her.

realization_account.text: Given to Jayadeva by her father at Jagannātha's command; her fidelity was tested when a queen told her falsely that Jayadeva had died, and she fell dead, to be revived by his singing.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Kumbhakarṇa (Mahārāṇā Kumbhā of Mewar)
summary: Rājput king and musicologist who wrote the Rasikapriyā commentary on the Gīta Govinda.

name: Mānaveda
summary: Zamorin prince-poet of Calicut who wrote the Kṛṣṇagīti on the model of the Gīta Govinda, basis of the Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam of Guruvāyūr.
